internship.title: Ethical Hacking & Cybersecurity Internship
internship.description: An industry-oriented cybersecurity internship focused on authorized security assessment. Interns progress from scope and rules of engagement through network reconnaissance, web application testing, vulnerability validation, controlled exploitation in dedicated labs, packet and host evidence analysis, security automation, professional reporting, and a final constrained assessment-tool project. The internship emphasizes evidence-backed reasoning, safe lab practice, testing, Git workflow, remediation, and retesting rather than indiscriminate scanning or exploit collection. It is suitable for learners who already understand basic Linux, networking, Python, and web concepts and want hands-on penetration-testing and defensive-analysis experience within explicitly authorized environments.
internship.durationRationale: Approximately 128 hours: guided study, lab setup, practical work, module engineering tasks, reporting exercises, and the final project/retest cycle. The duration is workload-based rather than tied to a calendar internship length.
prerequisites: Basic Linux command-line use: files, permissions, processes, pipes, and package installation.
Basic networking: IPv4 addressing, TCP/UDP, ports, DNS, HTTP/HTTPS, and common service protocols.
Basic programming: Python syntax, functions, exceptions, lists/dictionaries, and reading JSON.
Basic web concepts: requests, responses, headers, cookies, sessions, and HTML/JavaScript fundamentals.
A working virtualization environment capable of running a Linux security workstation and isolated lab targets.
A strict understanding that all scanning and exploitation activities in this internship are limited to owned or explicitly authorized systems.
objectives: Plan and execute authorized security assessments with precise scope and rules of engagement.
Perform network and web reconnaissance and turn observations into a structured attack-surface inventory.
Use Nmap, Burp Suite, Wireshark, and Metasploit appropriately in controlled environments.
Test authentication, authorization, input handling, security configuration, and common web vulnerability classes in legal training labs.
Validate scanner findings, manage false positives, document evidence, and design remediation retests.
Analyze packet and host evidence and map supported behaviors to a common threat vocabulary.
Build a constrained Python security utility with target policy enforcement, structured findings, automated tests, and reports.
Communicate findings clearly enough for another engineer to reproduce, remediate, and retest them.

modules.title: Ethical Hacking Foundations and Assessment Discipline
modules.description: Build the habits that distinguish authorized security testing from indiscriminate scanning: precise scope, repeatable methodology, evidence discipline, and professional conduct.
objectives: Plan an authorized assessment before touching a target.
Document scope, exclusions, evidence, and stop conditions.
Use a repeatable methodology rather than ad-hoc tool use.

lessons.title: Ethical Hacking Scope, Authorization, and Rules of Engagement
lessons.description: Establish the legal and operational boundary for security testing before any technical action. The intern learns to translate a request into a precise scope, exclusions, communication plan, and stop conditions.
learningObjectives: Explain why authorization and scope are prerequisites to technical testing.
Draft an assessment scope that names assets, exclusions, permitted techniques, and stop conditions.
Separate evidence collection from unauthorized discovery outside scope.

notes.text: Authorization is part of the technical design

A penetration test is not defined only by its tools. The target set, permitted techniques, maintenance window, data-handling expectations, communication path, and stopping conditions determine what technical actions are acceptable.

items: A workable rules-of-engagement document should identify:

notes.text: Never infer authorization from network reachability. A host responding to a packet is not evidence that it may be tested.

summary: Treat scope as a security control, not paperwork.
Begin with the least invasive method that can answer the assessment question.
Record evidence so another analyst can reproduce the finding.

quiz.question: Which item belongs in a rules-of-engagement document?
options: A guessed password list for an unrelated host
A public IP discovered by chance
quiz.explanation: Explicit exclusions reduce the chance that testing spills beyond authorized boundaries.

lessons.title: Assessment Methodology and Evidence Discipline
lessons.description: Use a repeatable assessment lifecycle: planning, discovery, validation, analysis, reporting, and remediation verification. The focus is on producing evidence, not collecting tool output for its own sake.
learningObjectives: Describe a repeatable security-testing lifecycle.
Choose evidence that supports or refutes a finding.
Record commands, timestamps, target identifiers, and observations for reproducibility.

notes.text: Evidence quality

A screenshot can be useful, but a strong finding preserves enough structured information to reproduce the test: target, request or command, relevant response or observation, date and time, and the reasoning that connects evidence to risk.

items: HTTP request/response excerpts with sensitive values redacted
Nmap service and version output from the approved scope
packet captures tied to a test step
application screenshots paired with request details
hashes or filenames for collected artifacts

notes.text: Do not retain secrets, session tokens, or personal data in a report unless the assessment explicitly requires it and the handling process permits it.

summary: A finding is a conclusion backed by evidence, not a scanner alert.

tasks.title: Draft a Rules-of-Engagement Document for an Isolated Lab
tasks.description: Create a one-page assessment boundary for an isolated lab containing a Linux attacker workstation and an intentionally vulnerable target.
tasks.problemStatement: A training team needs a security test that can be repeated safely. Define the target range, exclusions, time window, allowed techniques, stop conditions, and evidence-handling rules before scanning.
objectives: Write explicit scope and exclusions.
Define safe test limits and stop conditions.
Specify evidence handling and reporting expectations.
constraints: Use only a lab address range; do not include public targets.
No credential collection or persistence activities.
tasks.hint: Start by writing what is in scope, what is out of scope, when testing occurs, and when testing must stop.
tasks.solutionCode:
Scope: 192.168.56.0/24
In-scope assets: 192.168.56.101 (intentionally vulnerable lab VM)
Out of scope: host operating system, home/office networks, public internet hosts, and any address not explicitly listed
Testing window: 10:00-12:00 local lab time
Allowed: host discovery, TCP service enumeration, manual web testing, safe validation of intentionally vulnerable services
Prohibited: denial-of-service testing, persistence, destructive payloads, credential attacks against non-lab accounts
Stop conditions: unexpected instability, evidence of impact outside the lab VM, or any indication that a non-authorized asset is being reached
Evidence: store only the minimum data required; redact credentials and session tokens
Reporting: record target, method, timestamp, evidence, risk, remediation, and retest status
tasks.solutionExplanation: The document makes authorization operational. The explicit target and exclusion list prevent scope creep, while stop conditions define when technical work must pause.

deliverables: Initial Git repository with assessment notes
modules.assessment: The intern must produce a scope document that another tester could use without guessing the authorized targets or limits.

modules.title: Network Reconnaissance and Attack-Surface Mapping
modules.description: Develop an evidence-backed view of the network and web surface using Nmap and protocol knowledge, with increasing scan depth only when justified.
objectives: Enumerate services safely in an isolated lab.
Build a structured attack-surface inventory.
Connect network observations to application testing hypotheses.

lessons.title: Networking for Security Testing
lessons.description: Refresh IPv4 addressing, TCP and UDP behavior, common ports, DNS, ARP, and the meaning of a listening service. Connect packet behavior to what a scanner can and cannot infer.
learningObjectives: Explain how IP addresses, ports, and protocols combine to expose services.
Interpret basic TCP connection states during enumeration.
Distinguish a network-level observation from an application-level conclusion.

notes.text: Scanner output is an observation

A TCP port reported as open means a TCP connection can be established under the scan conditions. It does not, by itself, prove the exact application, patch level, or vulnerability. Service identification adds another layer of evidence.

TCP mental model:
client -> SYN -> server
server -> SYN/ACK -> client
client -> ACK -> established connection

summary: Ports identify transport endpoints; they do not inherently identify risk.
UDP requires different reasoning because lack of response is often ambiguous.
Service fingerprinting must be validated against application behavior.

quiz.question: What does an open TCP port primarily tell an assessor?
options: The host is an operating system server
quiz.explanation: An open-port result is evidence about reachability at the transport layer; more testing is needed to identify the application and risk.

lessons.title: Nmap Discovery, Service Enumeration, and Safe Scan Design
lessons.description: Use Nmap to build a disciplined service inventory in an authorized lab. Learn host discovery, focused port scanning, service detection, output capture, and how scan intensity affects reliability and load.
learningObjectives: Run focused Nmap scans against a lab target.
Capture results in machine-readable or reviewable form.
Explain why scan scope and timing matter.

notes.text: Representative lab workflow
For a single authorized lab VM, begin with a light service inventory and increase depth only when the previous evidence justifies it.

summary: Prefer narrowly scoped scans before broad scans.
Use saved output so findings can be reviewed later.
Treat version strings as leads that require validation.

practicals.title: Build a Lab Service Inventory with Nmap
practicals.description: Enumerate the services exposed by a single intentionally vulnerable lab VM and turn the output into a small attack-surface table.
steps: Confirm the target IP belongs to your isolated lab.
Run a TCP scan against a defined port range.
Run focused service detection against the ports discovered.
Save results with Nmap's output options.
Record port, protocol, service, version evidence, and follow-up validation questions.
practicals.solution: Use the commands in the lesson, then construct a table with columns Target, Port, Protocol, Service, Version Evidence, Validation Needed.
practicals.output: Expected behavior: Nmap returns a list of reachable services. The inventory should distinguish observed values from hypotheses that still need validation.

lessons.title: HTTP, DNS, TLS, and Web Reconnaissance
lessons.description: Map the web attack surface by identifying hosts, paths, methods, headers, cookies, redirects, and TLS properties without jumping directly to exploitation.
learningObjectives: Interpret HTTP request and response components relevant to security testing.
Identify web entry points and server-side redirects.
Capture reconnaissance evidence without exposing secrets in notes.

notes.text: Map before you mutate

A useful web reconnaissance pass identifies the application's reachable entry points, parameters, authentication boundaries, technology indicators, and security-relevant headers. The goal is to understand the surface before sending intrusive test payloads.

items: What hosts and ports serve HTTP(S)?
Which cookies are issued and with what security attributes?
Where does authentication begin and end?
What redirects and trust boundaries exist?

summary: HTTP metadata can reveal architecture without proving a vulnerability.
TLS protects the connection but does not make the application secure by itself.
DNS answers must be interpreted within the assessment scope.

tasks.title: Turn Nmap Output into an Attack-Surface Inventory
tasks.description: Convert raw scan observations into a prioritized list of validation questions.
tasks.problemStatement: A raw scan has been saved for an authorized lab host. You must distinguish confirmed services from assumptions and identify which observations require manual validation.
objectives: Separate evidence from inference.
Prioritize high-value services for manual validation.
Record follow-up questions for the web and service layers.
constraints: Use only the supplied lab target.
tasks.hint: For each service, ask what the service is, what evidence supports the identification, and what security property must be checked next.
tasks.solutionCode:
Target: 192.168.56.101
Evidence: TCP/80 open; service detection identifies an HTTP server
Validation question: enumerate application entry points and response headers
Evidence: TCP/445 open; service detection identifies SMB-related service
Validation question: identify whether guest access or unnecessary exposure is configured in the lab
Priority rule: validate externally reachable administrative or sensitive services before low-value informational services
tasks.solutionExplanation: The solution avoids treating scanner output as a final vulnerability list. It turns each observation into a specific, testable next step.

modules.assessment: The intern is assessed on whether each priority item is linked to observable evidence and a specific follow-up test.

modules.description: Move from web traffic observation to structured application testing: proxy analysis, authentication and authorization, injection classes, browser trust boundaries, misconfiguration, and secure evidence capture.
objectives: Analyze HTTP traffic systematically.

lessons.title: Burp Suite Workflow and HTTP Message Analysis
lessons.description: Use a web proxy to inspect and repeat requests in a legal lab. Learn how to identify parameters, cookies, authentication state, and server-side decisions from HTTP messages.
learningObjectives: Capture an HTTP request and response through a proxy.
Use Repeater-style manual iteration to test one variable at a time.
Explain the security relevance of methods, parameters, cookies, and status codes.

notes.text: Change one variable, record one observation

Manual testing becomes difficult to reason about when multiple request components change at once. Keep a stable baseline request, alter a single parameter or header, and compare the response. This creates a defensible chain from test input to observed behavior.

items: user A vs user B resource identifier

lessons.title: Authentication, Session Management, and Access Control Testing
lessons.description: Test identity and authorization boundaries without confusing authentication with authorization. Practice horizontal and vertical access-control checks in controlled applications.
learningObjectives: Differentiate authentication, session management, and authorization.
Design a horizontal access-control test between two lab users.
Design a vertical authorization test for a privileged endpoint.

notes.text: Authentication is not authorization

Authentication answers who the system believes the requester is. Authorization decides whether that identity may perform an action on a resource. A valid session therefore does not imply access to every resource.

items: Object ownership: replace one resource identifier with another user's identifier.
Privilege boundary: call a privileged endpoint with a low-privilege account.
Server-side enforcement: verify that access is denied even if the client UI hides a button.

quiz.question: Which test most directly checks horizontal authorization?
options: Use an authenticated low-privilege user to access another user's record
quiz.answer: Use an authenticated low-privilege user to access another user's record
quiz.explanation: Horizontal authorization concerns access between users with comparable privilege levels, such as ownership of another user's resource.

practicals.title: Test an Authorization Boundary in a Training Web App
practicals.description: Use two lab identities to determine whether one user can access another user's resource, then document the result and the expected control.
steps: Create or use two non-privileged accounts in an authorized training application.
Capture a legitimate resource request for user A.
Repeat the request as user B while changing only the resource identifier.
Compare the response status and body behavior.
Record whether server-side authorization prevented access.
Write remediation guidance focused on server-side object-level authorization.
practicals.solution: Baseline: authenticated request made by user A for resource R-A. Test: authenticate as user B and request R-A without changing any other trust decision. A secure application should reject the request if B does not own R-A.
practicals.output: Expected behavior: either an authorization denial (commonly 403, or an application-specific safe response) or a response that contains no unauthorized data. Do not claim a vulnerability unless the lab behavior actually permits unauthorized access.

lessons.title: Injection, XSS, CSRF, SSRF, and Input Validation in Labs
lessons.description: Understand how input crosses trust boundaries and how to validate or encode it. Use intentionally vulnerable training applications for controlled demonstrations of injection and browser/server-side request issues.
learningObjectives: Explain the difference between source input, processing context, and output encoding.
Recognize common injection classes and their defensive control patterns.
Use legal training labs to reproduce a vulnerability and document the evidence.

notes.text: Context matters

Injection vulnerabilities occur when data is interpreted as instructions in a context that was not intended. The defensive control depends on the context: parameterized SQL queries for SQL injection, contextual output encoding for XSS, strict allowlists and network controls for SSRF, and anti-CSRF mechanisms for state-changing browser requests.
Do not test these techniques against systems you do not own or lack explicit permission to assess. Use dedicated training labs such as PortSwigger Web Security Academy for practice.

A secure application depends on more than code. Debug mode, verbose stack traces, exposed source maps, directory listings, unsafe file types, default credentials, or unnecessary management interfaces can create paths around otherwise sound application logic.

items: error messages with sensitive details redacted

tasks.title: Write a Reproducible Web Authorization Finding
tasks.description: Document a controlled access-control issue from a training application as a professional finding.
tasks.problemStatement: A lab application returns another user's record when a resource identifier is changed. Produce a reproducible finding with evidence, impact, root cause hypothesis, remediation, and retest criteria.
objectives: Record the exact preconditions and request flow.
Explain the difference between authentication and authorization.
Provide a server-side remediation strategy and regression test.
requirements: Burp Suite or browser developer tools
constraints: Do not include real personal data in the report.
tasks.hint: Start with the baseline request. The strongest evidence changes only the identity or object identifier relevant to the authorization decision.
tasks.solutionCode:
Finding: Object-level authorization failure in a controlled lab
Precondition: two non-privileged lab accounts exist
Reproduction: user A requests object A successfully; user B replays the same object identifier while authenticated as user B
Observed result: the lab returns object A to user B
Impact: a user may access data they do not own
Root-cause hypothesis: authorization is not enforced on the server for object ownership
Remediation: authorize every object access on the server using the authenticated principal and object ownership/role policy
Regression test: user B requests object A and must receive an authorization denial or equivalent safe response
tasks.solutionExplanation: The finding ties identity, resource ownership, observed response, and remediation together. The report does not assume a real-world impact beyond what the controlled lab demonstrates.

modules.assessment: A reviewer should be able to reproduce the finding from the intern's steps without guessing the request sequence.

modules.title: Vulnerability Validation, Risk, and Professional Reporting
modules.description: Develop the judgment needed to turn scanner signals and manual observations into validated, prioritized findings with actionable remediation and retest criteria.
objectives: Validate findings rather than blindly trust scanner alerts.
Produce evidence-backed risk statements.
Design retests that verify security controls after remediation.

lessons.title: Vulnerability Scanners, CVEs, and False Positives
lessons.description: Learn how scanners accelerate discovery but do not replace validation. Interpret vulnerability identifiers, affected versions, evidence quality, and false-positive conditions.
learningObjectives: Explain why a CVE identifier is not itself proof of exploitability.
Validate a scanner finding against service identity and configuration evidence.
Record false-positive reasons and close the evidence loop.

notes.text: Signal versus finding

A scanner can detect a pattern, version, response, or configuration that correlates with risk. A professional assessor still confirms that the detected component is actually present, that the finding applies to the target configuration, and that the evidence is sufficient.

lessons.description: Turn technical evidence into a useful security finding with clear impact, likelihood reasoning, remediation, evidence, and retest guidance. Avoid unsupported severity inflation.
learningObjectives: Write concise finding titles and evidence-backed impact statements.
Choose severity using the actual conditions demonstrated by the lab or assessment.

notes.text: A strong finding answers five questions
What is wrong? Where is it? How was it verified? Why does it matter? What should be changed and how will the fix be retested?

quiz.question: Which evidence is strongest for a verified access-control issue?
options: A scanner says 'possible access control issue'
A reproducible request from an unauthorized lab user returns the protected object
quiz.answer: A reproducible request from an unauthorized lab user returns the protected object
quiz.explanation: A reproducible observation directly demonstrates the security control failure in the assessed environment.

lessons.title: Remediation Verification and Retesting
lessons.description: Treat retesting as a new evidence exercise: reproduce the prior condition, confirm the control now behaves correctly, and verify that the fix did not shift the issue elsewhere.
learningObjectives: Design a regression test from an original finding.
Compare before-and-after evidence without assuming the fix worked.
Document residual risk and retest scope.

notes.text: Retest the control, not only the symptom

A remediation might remove an obvious endpoint while leaving an alternate route, method, or object reference exposed. A retest should therefore reproduce the original proof and then probe the same security property through closely related paths within scope.

Do not perform destructive validation simply to increase confidence. A safe, reproducible test is preferred to an intrusive one when the security property can be demonstrated without additional impact.

tasks.title: Triage a Mixed Vulnerability Scan
tasks.description: Review a fictional lab scan containing confirmed, unconfirmed, and irrelevant observations and produce a prioritized triage list.
tasks.problemStatement: A scanner reports five findings on an intentionally vulnerable lab VM. One is confirmed, two require validation, one is a false positive, and one is out of scope. Create a triage decision for each item.
objectives: Classify evidence quality.
Identify which findings require manual validation.
Reject out-of-scope work without technical action.
tasks.hint: For each alert, record what the evidence proves, what it does not prove, and what the next safe step should be.
tasks.solutionCode:
Alert 1: HTTP directory listing observed -> Confirmed configuration observation -> Report with evidence and remediation
Alert 2: Old software version reported without banner validation -> Needs validation -> Confirm service/version evidence
Alert 3: CVE match based only on guessed package version -> Needs validation -> Obtain authoritative version evidence before severity assignment

Alert 5: Port shown open in historical output but closed during retest -> Historical signal only -> Revalidate before reporting

5. Run the module's check action when supported.
6. If the check supports the hypothesis and the lab scope permits exploitation, run the minimum validation action.
7. Record the achieved result and privilege level without collecting unrelated data.
8. Close the session and restore the lab to its expected state.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The solution treats exploitation as a validation step following reconnaissance, not as the first activity. It also defines a bounded target and a cleanup step.

project.heading: Build an Authorized Lab Security Assessment Toolkit
project.name: Authorized Lab Security Assessment Toolkit
project.description: Build a small, reviewable Python security-assessment utility for private or loopback laboratory web targets. The toolkit validates the target policy before making any request, performs non-destructive HTTP header and cookie checks, inspects the negotiated TLS version when HTTPS is used, performs bounded TCP connect checks for an explicit port list, and produces structured JSON plus an HTML report. The project is intentionally narrower than a full scanner: its engineering value is the combination of scope enforcement, repeatability, evidence, testing, and reporting.
project.problemStatement: Security teams need repeatable ways to verify a limited set of web-security controls in development and test environments. Manual checks are easy to forget or record inconsistently. The intern must build a constrained utility that can be run against an authorized lab target and produce a traceable set of observations without embedding credentials, exploit payloads, persistence, stealth, or unrestricted target discovery.
objectives: Implement an allowlist policy that accepts only HTTP/HTTPS URLs resolving to private or loopback addresses.
Collect non-destructive response-header and cookie evidence.
Inspect negotiated TLS protocol information for HTTPS targets.
Perform bounded TCP connection checks for explicitly selected ports.
Normalize observations as typed findings and export them to JSON and HTML.
Write automated tests for target policy and output encoding.
Document limitations, threat model, safe-use rules, and retest procedure.
requirements: Python 3 with access to the standard library.
An authorized HTTP or HTTPS lab target bound to loopback or a private IP range.
A terminal capable of running Python's unittest discovery.
Git for source control and reviewable commits.
The assessment must be non-destructive and state-free: the tool uses GET/connection checks only and does not submit credentials or mutate application data.

All redirects encountered during an HTTP check must be treated according to the target-policy decision; a production implementation should validate every redirect destination before following it. The provided project keeps the request surface intentionally small.
The project must not log secrets, cookies' secret values, authorization headers, or request bodies.
features: Target policy enforcement: parse URL, restrict scheme, resolve host, and reject destinations that are not private or loopback.
Security-header checks: report selected missing response security headers as low-severity observations with remediation guidance.
Cookie attribute checks: identify missing Secure and HttpOnly attributes where relevant to the observed Set-Cookie response.
TLS inspection: report negotiated TLS version and identify legacy TLS 1.0/1.1 negotiations if the environment actually permits them.
Bounded port checks: connect to an explicit user-provided list of TCP ports without scanning an unbounded range.
Structured findings: use stable identifiers, severity, target, description, evidence, remediation, and status.
Machine-readable and human-readable output: JSON and HTML reports are generated from the same findings model.
Automated policy and reporting tests: verify private-target acceptance, public-target rejection, unsupported scheme rejection, JSON content, and HTML escaping.

from __future__ import annotations

import socket
import ssl

from .models import Finding
from .policy import validate_target


def inspect_tls(url: str, timeout: float = 5.0) -> list[Finding]:
    scheme, hostname, port = validate_target(url)
    if scheme != "https":
        return []
    findings: list[Finding] = []
    context = ssl.create_default_context()
    try:
        with socket.create_connection((hostname, port), timeout=timeout) as raw:
            with context.wrap_socket(raw, server_hostname=hostname) as tls_socket:
                version = tls_socket.version()
                cipher = tls_socket.cipher()
                if version is None:
                    findings.append(
                        Finding(
                            id="TLS-VERSION-UNKNOWN",
                            title="TLS version could not be determined",
                            severity="info",
                            target=url,
                            description="The TLS socket did not expose a negotiated version.",
                            evidence="TLS version=None",
                            remediation="Verify the service's TLS configuration using the authoritative server configuration and deployment documentation.",
                            status="informational",
                        )
                    )
                if version in {"TLSv1", "TLSv1.1"}:
                    findings.append(
                        Finding(
                            id="TLS-LEGACY",
                            title=f"Legacy TLS version negotiated: {version}",
                            severity="high",
                            target=url,
                            description="The service negotiated a legacy TLS protocol version.",
                            evidence=f"Negotiated TLS version={version}; cipher={cipher[0] if cipher else 'unknown'}",
                            remediation="Disable legacy TLS protocol versions and follow the deployment platform's supported TLS configuration guidance.",
                        )
                    )
    except (OSError, ssl.SSLError) as exc:
        findings.append(
            Finding(
                id="TLS-CONNECTION",
                title="TLS connection could not be established",
                severity="info",
                target=url,
                description="The TLS check could not complete.",
                evidence=f"Exception type={type(exc).__name__}",
                remediation="Review reachability, certificate configuration, and service logs before treating this as a security finding.",
                status="informational",
            )
        )
    return findings

from __future__ import annotations

import socket

from .models import Finding
from .policy import validate_target


def check_ports(url: str, ports: list[int], timeout: float = 1.5) -> list[Finding]:
    scheme, hostname, _ = validate_target(url)
    findings: list[Finding] = []
    for port in ports:
        if not (1 <= port <= 65535):
            raise ValueError(f"Invalid TCP port: {port}")
        try:
            with socket.create_connection((hostname, port), timeout=timeout):
                severity = "info"
                findings.append(
                    Finding(
                        id=f"PORT-{port}",
                        title=f"TCP port {port} is reachable",
                        severity=severity,
                        target=f"{scheme}://{hostname}:{port}",
                        description="A TCP connection was established to the requested port.",
                        evidence=f"TCP connect succeeded to {hostname}:{port}",
                        remediation="Review whether the service should be reachable from the assessed network segment.",
                        status="informational",
                    )
                )
        except (OSError, TimeoutError):
            continue
    return findings

    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Controlled security assessment for private or loopback lab targets")
    parser.add_argument("url", help="HTTP or HTTPS URL for an authorized lab target")
    parser.add_argument("--ports", default="80,443", help="Comma-separated TCP ports to test")
    parser.add_argument("--timeout", type=float, default=5.0)
    parser.add_argument("--output", type=Path, default=Path("assessment-output"))
    return parser


def main() -> int:
    parser = build_parser()
    args = parser.parse_args()
    ports = [int(value.strip()) for value in args.ports.split(",") if value.strip()]
    findings = []
    findings.extend(inspect_headers(args.url, timeout=args.timeout))
    findings.extend(inspect_cookies(args.url, timeout=args.timeout))
    findings.extend(inspect_tls(args.url, timeout=args.timeout))
    findings.extend(check_ports(args.url, ports=ports, timeout=min(args.timeout, 2.0)))
    json_path, html_path = write_reports(findings, args.output)
    print(f"JSON report: {json_path}")
    print(f"HTML report: {html_path}")
    print(f"Findings: {len(findings)}")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

import unittest

from security_audit.policy import TargetPolicyError, validate_target


class TargetPolicyTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_loopback_is_allowed(self):
        scheme, host, port = validate_target("http://127.0.0.1:8000")
        self.assertEqual(scheme, "http")
        self.assertEqual(host, "127.0.0.1")
        self.assertEqual(port, 8000)

    def test_https_default_port(self):
        scheme, host, port = validate_target("https://127.0.0.1")
        self.assertEqual(scheme, "https")
        self.assertEqual(host, "127.0.0.1")
        self.assertEqual(port, 443)

    def test_public_ip_is_rejected(self):
        with self.assertRaises(TargetPolicyError):
            validate_target("http://8.8.8.8")

    def test_bad_scheme_is_rejected(self):
        with self.assertRaises(TargetPolicyError):
            validate_target("ftp://127.0.0.1")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()

fileWiseSolution.code:
# Authorized Lab Security Assessment Toolkit

This project is intentionally constrained to private or loopback HTTP(S) targets. It performs non-destructive GET-based header/cookie checks, basic TLS inspection, and bounded TCP connect checks. It emits JSON and HTML evidence for an assessment workflow.

## Run tests

python -m unittest discover -s tests -v

## Run the assessment

python main.py http://127.0.0.1:8000 --ports 8000,8080 --output assessment-output

The policy layer rejects public addresses and unsupported schemes before network requests are made. Do not modify the policy to bypass the authorization boundary.

fileWiseSolution.explanation: Keeps Python cache files and generated assessment output out of source control.

project.howItWorks: The user supplies one HTTP(S) lab URL and an explicit list of TCP ports. The CLI calls the target policy before each check. The policy resolves the hostname and rejects any IP that is not private or loopback. The HTTP layer performs a bounded GET and evaluates selected response headers and cookie attributes. The TLS layer creates a TLS connection for HTTPS targets and records the negotiated version. The network layer performs bounded TCP connects only for the explicitly supplied ports. Each check returns Finding objects. The reporting layer serializes those objects to JSON and escaped HTML.
project.dataFlow: User input -> argparse -> target policy -> HTTP/TLS/TCP checks -> Finding objects -> report serializer -> findings.json and report.html

cases: JSON report contains finding identifiers and severity

securityReview: The default policy rejects public destinations and unsupported schemes.
No credentials, authorization headers, or request bodies are sent.
HTTP and TCP operations use bounded timeouts.
The tool performs GET and connection checks only; it does not create, update, delete, or upload application data.
Generated HTML escapes all dynamic finding content.
Generated assessment output is excluded from Git by .gitignore.
The project is intentionally not a generalized vulnerability scanner and does not implement exploitation, persistence, stealth, credential attacks, or unrestricted discovery.
performanceAndLimitations: Checks are sequential and intentionally small; the project prioritizes safety and reviewability over throughput.
DNS may return multiple addresses. The policy rejects the target if any resolved address is public, which is conservative but can also block mixed private/public infrastructure.
Header presence is not a complete evaluation of header quality; a present header can still be weak or incorrectly configured.
Cookie checks inspect observed Set-Cookie attributes but cannot determine business sensitivity of every cookie from the response alone.
TLS inspection is intentionally narrow and does not replace a complete TLS configuration review.
TCP reachability is not proof that a service is vulnerable.

troubleshooting.problem: The tool rejects a target with a policy error.
troubleshooting.cause: The hostname resolved to a public address or the URL scheme is unsupported.
troubleshooting.resolution: Use an authorized private or loopback lab target and confirm the URL uses HTTP or HTTPS.

troubleshooting.problem: The HTTP check fails with a timeout.
troubleshooting.cause: The lab service may be stopped, filtered, or too slow for the configured timeout.
troubleshooting.resolution: Confirm the service is reachable within the authorized lab and adjust the bounded timeout conservatively.

troubleshooting.problem: TLS check reports an informational connection failure.
troubleshooting.cause: Certificate or protocol negotiation may not be compatible with the local TLS configuration.
troubleshooting.resolution: Inspect the lab service certificate and TLS configuration separately; do not classify a failed check as a vulnerability without evidence.

troubleshooting.problem: HTML report does not show raw evidence markup.
troubleshooting.cause: The renderer escapes dynamic text by design.
troubleshooting.resolution: This is expected behavior and is part of the reporting security control.

passCriteria: All required files are present and consistent.
The tool rejects a public test target rather than connecting to it.
The authorized lab run produces JSON and HTML output.
The intern can explain the limits of each automated check and distinguish observations from confirmed vulnerabilities.
The intern demonstrates a safe retest after a controlled lab configuration change.

evaluation.approach: Competency-based review using work products, practical demonstrations, module tasks, and the final project.

criteria.name: Authorization discipline
criteria.evidence: Scope document explicitly lists assets, exclusions, allowed techniques, and stop conditions.

criteria.name: Technical execution
criteria.evidence: Commands and tooling are used accurately in controlled labs, with evidence captured for each claim.

criteria.name: Web security reasoning
criteria.evidence: The intern distinguishes authentication, authorization, validation, browser trust boundaries, and configuration risks.

criteria.name: Validation judgment
criteria.evidence: Scanner signals are verified or rejected rather than copied directly into a report.

criteria.name: Defensive reasoning
criteria.evidence: Traffic and host artifacts are correlated without overclaiming identity or intent.

criteria.name: Secure automation
criteria.evidence: The final tool enforces its own scope policy, uses bounded operations, and has automated tests.

criteria.name: Reporting
criteria.evidence: Findings contain reproducible evidence, realistic impact, remediation, and retest criteria.

criteria.name: Engineering practice
criteria.evidence: Git history, README, tests, and review notes make the work maintainable and reproducible.

finalReviewQuestions: What was explicitly in scope and what was excluded?
Which finding was verified manually, and what evidence supports it?
Which scan results were false positives or unresolved hypotheses?
How does the final project prevent public-target assessment?
What limitations prevent the project from being treated as a complete vulnerability scanner?
How would you retest one finding after remediation?

gitWorkflow: Create a repository before technical work so scope notes and evidence templates are versioned.
Use a branch per meaningful work item where practical.
Write commits that describe the security or engineering change rather than vague progress updates.
Do not commit generated reports containing sensitive data or session artifacts.
Use code review checkpoints before merging project changes.
ethicsAndSafety: All active testing in this internship is restricted to systems owned by the learner or explicitly authorized for assessment.
Public internet hosts are not training targets. Use intentionally vulnerable VMs and legal interactive labs for offensive exercises.

Avoid denial-of-service, destructive actions, persistence, credential spraying, stealth, or evasion unless a dedicated controlled lab exercise explicitly teaches the underlying concept and the target is isolated and authorized.
Prefer the least intrusive technique that answers the assessment question.
Redact passwords, tokens, personal data, and other secrets from evidence before sharing it.

deprecatedOrLegacyNotes.note: Legacy TLS versions should not be taught as current security practice. The final project treats TLS 1.0/1.1 negotiation as a finding when the actual environment permits it, while modern deployments should follow currently supported platform guidance.
Treating exploitation as the first step is poor assessment practice. The internship emphasizes scope, reconnaissance, validation, and minimum-impact proof before exploitation.

studentCompletenessTest: The intern can state exactly what systems they are authorized to test.
The intern can produce a network and web attack-surface inventory supported by tool evidence.
The intern can reproduce at least one web security issue in a legal training lab and explain the security control that failed.
The intern can distinguish a scanner signal from a verified vulnerability.
The intern can analyze a traffic or host-evidence scenario without overstating certainty.
The intern can build and explain a constrained security utility with automated tests.
The intern can write a finding that another engineer could reproduce, remediate, and retest.
The intern can explain the limits of the tools and checks they used.
